one_liner: Meta's JIT virtual machine for Hack; reported 1.6x over the 2014-era Zend PHP interpreter on real applications.
what_it_does: HHVM runs Hack programs: a frontend (OCaml and Rust: the hackc compiler crate) turns source into HipHop bytecode (HHBC), optionally optimized ahead of time by HHBBC into a '.hhbc' repo, and the C++ runtime interprets or JIT-compiles it. It ships as a standalone 'hhvm' binary that runs scripts directly (hhvm example.hack) or serves web requests through its built-in Proxygen server or FastCGI behind nginx/Apache. It is not a library and, since HHVM 4.0 (2019), not a PHP engine.
how_it_is_fast: A type-specializing JIT: it observes the runtime types flowing through bytecode, emits machine code specialized for them and guards the assumptions with type checks. Code is first compiled as small 'tracelet' profiling regions, then retranslated with profile-guided optimization into large 'hot CFG' regions that can cover whole functions with loops. Regions are lowered HHBC to HHIR (SSA IR with a rich type lattice, guard relaxation, simplification, dead-code elimination) to vasm (low-level IR with its own register allocator) and then to x86-64 or arm64 code; HHBBC whole-program type inference in repo-authoritative mode removes more checks ahead of time.
when_to_use: You write Hack (or are migrating a large PHP 5-era codebase into Hack) and want a JIT VM tuned for a long-running, request-oriented web tier like Meta's.
Large server-side codebases where a repo-authoritative (whole-program, pre-compiled bytecode) deployment and profile-guided warm-up are acceptable.
Studying a production dynamic-language JIT: the hackers-guide docs and the region-based PGO design (PLDI 2018) are a good reference for type-specializing JITs.
x86-64 servers with AVX2-class CPUs (the build uses -march=x86-64-v3) or aarch64 Linux.
when_not_to_use: Running PHP: the 3.30 series was the last that aimed for PHP compatibility and HHVM 4.0 (2019) is Hack-only (search snippets of hhvm.com and Phoronix; the pages were blocked here); for PHP use php-src with opcache JIT, the catalogued PHP JIT sibling.

You need packaged, versioned releases: the GitHub repo has no tags after HHVM-4.172.3 and HHVM-4.168.4 (both 2023-05-02) even though master gets commits daily, so current code means building from source (the hackers guide warns the first build can take an hour or more).
Short-lived CLI scripts or small sites: the JIT relies on profiling then retranslation, so warm-up matters; startup and memory cost are not documented in the repo.
Pre-Haswell x86-64 CPUs, 32-bit systems, or PIE-only environments: CMake forces -march=x86-64-v3, refuses non-64-bit builds and links with -no-pie.
Licence-sensitive redistribution: the core is PHP-3.01 plus Zend-2.0 (not OSI-approved); only the Hack typechecker and HSL are MIT.

integration.form: standalone VM binary with built-in web server (not a library)
integration.dependencies: large: folly, fizz, wangle, mvfst, proxygen, fbthrift, mcrouter, Boost, OpenSSL, ICU, PCRE, RE2, libevent, libxml2, libsodium, libdwarf, libelf, libunwind, TBB, oniguruma and others (CMake/HPHPFindLibs.cmake, third-party/); OCaml via opam/dune and Rust/Cargo for the Hack frontend
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (CMakeLists.txt), CMake 3.18+, GCC or Clang; hackc crate uses Rust edition 2024 (so Rust 1.85 or newer)
integration.platforms: 64-bit Linux on x86-64 (built with -march=x86-64-v3) and aarch64; macOS has CMake handling (deployment target 10.15) but support level is not documented here
integration.thread_safety: multi-threaded server; each request runs in its own request context, and process-wide state such as setlocale() leaks across requests (hphp/doc/limitations)

gotchas: The only speed numbers are first-party and snippet-only: the OOPSLA 2014 paper (1.6x over PHP on real-world apps in sandbox mode; 2.64x and 2.79x geomean on its benchmark suite vs HPHPc's 1.93x) and the PLDI 2018 JIT paper (21.7% faster on the Facebook website than the previous tracelet-based HHVM JIT, per a review snippet); neither paper was opened here, and the repo carries no benchmark.

The PHP baseline is obsolete: it is the 2014-era Zend interpreter, before PHP 7 rewrote the engine and PHP 8 added a JIT, and current HHVM no longer runs PHP, so no current like-for-like comparison exists. Meta's own oss-performance harness (hhvm/oss-performance: WordPress, Drupal, MediaWiki and others on PHP 5, PHP 7 and HHVM) was archived on 2022-01-13 with the README saying it had no results to share.

In-repo docs are partly stale: hphp/doc/hackers-guide says HHVM is written in C++14 and that PHP is 'currently supported for historical reasons', while CMakeLists.txt requires C++20 and PHP support ended in 2019; jit-core.md still lists a ppc64 backend, but the CMake files only detect x86_64 and aarch64.

Type guards multiply: without guard relaxation, a translation with 4 guards can need up to 10^4 retranslations that chain linearly (jit-optimizations.md), so highly polymorphic code can fall off the fast path.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick HHVM only for Hack code; for PHP the php-src opcache JIT (catalogued at about 2.6x-9.5x faster than plain PHP 8.2 on kostya/jit-benchmarks numeric kernels, derived from its sibling summary) and JPHP (claims about 13% slower than PHP 7.4) are the relevant siblings, and current HHVM cannot run PHP at all. Compared with Meta's other catalogued JIT, Cinder (CPython), HHVM is the far more mature, production-proven design but locks you into the Hack language.
verified_claims_summary: No numbers exist in the repo; the claim rests on search snippets of the peer-reviewed but first-party OOPSLA 2014 paper: HHVM about 1.6x faster than the PHP (Zend) interpreter of that time on real-world applications in sandbox mode, and 2.64x (sandbox) and 2.79x (production) geometric-mean speedups on its benchmark suite against 1.93x for the earlier HPHPc static compiler; PHP version, hardware and flags were not visible. A later first-party figure (PLDI 2018, snippet) is a 21.7% gain on the Facebook website from the region-based PGO JIT over HHVM's earlier tracelet JIT.
status_note: Very actively developed (commits on 2026-10-06) as Meta's production Hack runtime, but with no GitHub release tags since May 2023, a heavyweight from-source build and a mixed PHP/Zend licence, it is practical only for teams committed to Hack.
